metadata.title: Numerical simulations of X-rays Free Electron Lasers (XFEL)

nodes.name: XFEL nonlinear Schrodinger equation (first-principles model)
nodes.statement: The fundamental model for XFEL is the following nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation \beq \left\{ \begin{aligned} &i\hbar\d_t\psi=\frac{1}{2m}(i\hbar\nabla-e\Ab)^2\psi+Ze\frac{1}{|\xb|}\psi+e^2(|\cdot|^{- 1}\ast|\psi|^2)\psi -\lambda|\psi|^\sigma\psi,\\ &\psi(t,\xb)|_{t=0}=\psi_0(\xb), \end{aligned}\right. \ee on $\mathbb{R}^3$. Here $m_e$ is the electron mass, $e$ the electron charge, $Z$ the atomic number and $\hbar$ is the scaled (by $2\pi$) Planck constant. The constant $\lambda>0$ measures the strenght of the local attractive nonlinearity with power $\sigma>0$, in particular $\sigma=\frac{2}{3}$ and $\lambda=3e^2\left(\frac{3}{8\pi}\right)^{1/3}$ for the local Hartree-Fock approximation.
nodes.statement_short: Cubic-type nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation with magnetic potential $\Ab$, Coulomb attraction to the nucleus, repulsive Hartree convolution and local attractive Fock nonlinearity $-\lambda|\psi|^\sigma\psi$.

nodes.name: External electromagnetic field depends on time only
nodes.statement: The vector field ${\Ab}={\Ab}(t)$ represents an external electromagnetic field, which we shall assume to depend on time $t$ only (not on position $\xb$).

nodes.name: Systematic justification of an effective time-averaged magnetic field
nodes.statement: In the experimental setup of interest \cite{Ch,frat1} the magnetic field is rapidly oscillating. This effect of oscillating external magnetic field appears often in the modelling of undulators; here the aim is to justify systematically the use of an effective, time-averaged magnetic field, in the presence of beam-matter interaction.
nodes.statement_short: Justify replacing the rapidly oscillating external magnetic field by its time average in the presence of beam-matter interaction.

nodes.name: Semiclassical parameter
nodes.statement: Defining the semiclassical parameter $\eps=\frac{\hbar t_c}{2m_ex_c^2}$

nodes.name: Rescaled XFEL Schrodinger equation
nodes.statement: We scale the equation (1.1) by choosing a characteristic time scale $t_c$ and a characteristic spatial scale $x_c$. Defining the semiclassical parameter $\eps=\frac{\hbar t_c}{2m_ex_c^2}$ we obtain after rescaling \begin{equation*} i\eps\d_t\psi=(i\eps\nabla-\Ab)^2\psi+\frac{c}{|x|}\psi+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|\psi|^2)\psi-a|\psi|^\sigma\psi \end{equation*} where $c=eZ\frac{t_c^2}{2m_ex_c}$, $C_1=e^2\frac{t_c^6}{8m_e^3x_c^4}$, $a=\lambda\left(\frac{t_c^2}{2m_ex_c^2}\right)^{\sigma+1}$. Here also $\psi$ and $\Ab$ were scaled appropriately.
nodes.statement_short: Non-dimensionalized XFEL equation with semiclassical parameter $\eps$ and constants $c$, $C_1$, $a$.

nodes.name: Lens-type transform removing the magnetic potential
nodes.statement: A standard transform is used to simplify the original equation, and bring it to a form more amenable to analysis as well as computation. By setting \beq u(t,\xb) = \psi\(t, \xb + b(t)\) \exp\(\frac{i}{\eps}\dpm\int_0^t{|\Ab(s)|^2ds}\), \ee where $b(t)=2\int_0^t\Ab(s)ds$,
nodes.statement_short: Change of unknown by a moving frame shift $b(t)$ plus a phase factor, which eliminates the magnetic potential.

nodes.name: Initial value problem for the transformed wave function
nodes.statement: one readily checks that $u$ satisfies the initial value problem \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\eps\partial_tu=-\eps^2\Delta u+\frac{c}{|\xb-b(t)|} u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u -a|u|^\sigma u\\ &u^\omega(t,\xb)\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\xb), \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation} where $u_0:=\psi_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Transformed problem: no magnetic term, but a Coulomb potential centred at the moving point $b(t)$.

nodes.name: Choice of scales with eps=1 and sinusoidal shift b(t)
nodes.statement: Now we choose the scales $x_c, t_c$ such that $\eps=1$ (thus relating $x_c$ and $t_c$ by $2m_ex_c^2=\hbar t_c$), since we are mostly interested in the fully quantum mechanical case, and we fix \begin{equation*} b(t)=e(t)\sin(2\pi\omega t). \end{equation*} where $e:\R\to\R^3$ is a smooth vector field, slowly varying in time.
nodes.statement_short: Fully quantum scaling $\eps=1$ and shift $b(t)=e(t)\sin(2\pi\omega t)$ with slowly varying amplitude $e(t)$.

nodes.name: Large frequency regime
nodes.statement: We consider the large frequency case \begin{equation*} |\omega|\gg\frac{{\rm sec}}{t_c}=\frac{\hbar}{2m_e}\left(\frac{{\rm meter}}{x_c}\right)^2\approx 5\times10^{-3}\left(\frac{{\rm meter}}{x_c}\right)^2. \end{equation*} and study the asymptotic regime $|\omega|\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic regime of very large oscillation frequency $|\omega|\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Fast-potential model
nodes.statement: In particular we shall investigate the convergence of solutions of \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V^\omega u^\omega+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega\\ &u^\omega(t,\xb)\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\xb), \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The oscillatory (fast-potential) problem for $u^\omega$ with rapidly oscillating Coulomb potential $V^\omega$.

nodes.name: Fast oscillatory potential
nodes.statement: where the fast oscillatory potential is given by \begin{equation} V^\omega(t, x):=\frac{c}{|\xb-e(t)\sin(2\pi\omega t)|}, \end{equation}

nodes.name: Time-averaged (approximate) model
nodes.statement: to solutions of the approximate problem (see \cite{xfel1} and Theorem 1 there) \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u\\ &u(t,\xb)\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\xb), \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The effective problem obtained by replacing $V^\omega$ with its time average $\langle V\rangle$.

nodes.name: Time averaged potential
nodes.statement: with $\langle V\rangle$ is the time \emph{averaged} potential given by \begin{equation} \langle V\rangle(t, \xb):=\int_0^1\frac{c}{|\xb-e(t)\sin(2\pi s)|}ds. \end{equation} We remark that \eqref{eq:avr-p} is well defined as the weak limit of $V^\omega$ defined in \eqref{eq:fast-p} in the space $L^\infty(\R;L^{3-}(\R^3)+L^{3+}(\R^3))$, as $|\omega|\to\infty$ (see \cite{xfel1} for more details).
nodes.statement_short: One-period average of the oscillating Coulomb potential; the weak limit of $V^\omega$ as $|\omega|\to\infty$.
differentia: well defined as the weak limit of $V^\omega$ defined in \eqref{eq:fast-p} in the space $L^\infty(\R;L^{3-}(\R^3)+L^{3+}(\R^3))$, as $|\omega|\to\infty$

nodes.name: Physical magnitude of the frequency in molecular imaging
nodes.statement: In molecular imaging (spatial characteristic scale of the order of magnitude of thousand nanometers, temporal characteristic scale of some femtoseconds), we compute $\omega\gg10^{15}$. Therefore it makes sense to investigate the asymptotic regime. We shall demonstrate later on that this is reached already for much smaller values of $\omega$.

nodes.name: Averaging result for the XFEL Schrodinger equation (main result of [xfel1])
nodes.statement: Let $0<\sigma<4/3$, $u_0\in L^2(\R^3)$, $u^\omega, u\in C(\R; L^2(\R^3))$ be the unique global solutions of \eqref{eq:fast}, \eqref{eq:avr}, respectively. Then for each finite time $0<T<\infty$ and for each admissible Strichartz index pair $(q, r)$, we have \begin{equation*} \|u^\omega-u\|_{L^q([0, T]; L^r(\R^3))}\to0\qquad\textrm{as}\;|\omega|\to\infty. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: In the mass-subcritical range $\sigma<4/3$, solutions of the fast-potential model converge to those of the time-averaged model in every Strichartz norm as $|\omega|\to\infty$.
assumptions: $u^\omega, u\in C(\R; L^2(\R^3))$ be the unique global solutions of \eqref{eq:fast}, \eqref{eq:avr}, respectively
for each admissible Strichartz index pair $(q, r)$

nodes.name: Weak (not strong) convergence of the energy
nodes.statement: We use this averaging result as a benchmark (example \ref{ex1}); the energy for the fast problem is observed to converge weakly to the energy for the averaged problem (and not strongly $L^\infty$ in time).
nodes.statement_short: Numerically the fast-problem energy converges only weakly in time to the averaged-problem energy.
assumptions: the energy for the fast problem
conclusions: converge weakly to the energy for the averaged problem (and not strongly $L^\infty$ in time)

nodes.name: Time-splitting spectral algorithm
nodes.statement: We solve \eqref{eq:fast} or \eqref{eq:avr} by a classical time-splitting spectral scheme as follows \cite{BJM, HJMSZ}: \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \I \partial _t u_1 = -\, \btu u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{pseudo-spectral} method. Thus we can get the value of $u_1$ at new time $t^{n+1}$ by \[u^{n+1}_1=\(e^{-\I\btu t |\xi|^2}\hat{u}_1^{n}(\xi)\)^\vee,\] here `$\wedge$' and `$\vee$' denote the Fourier and inverse Fourier transform respectively. Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\xb)=|u_1(t^{n+1},\xb)|^2$, then we compute the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}(t^{n+1},\xb)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\] \textbf{Step 2.} We solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\I \partial _tu_2  = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\xb)-a|u_2|^\sg\right)u_2, \quad u_2(t^{n},\xb)=u_1(t^{n+1},\xb), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\xb)$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}. It is easy to check that in this step the density $\rho(t,\xb)\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\xb)$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\btu t,\xb)=u_2(t,\xb)\,\exp\({\dpm-\I \int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \left(C_1V_{Hartree}(\xb)+V(s,\xb)-a\rho^\frac{\sg}{2}(\xb)\right) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\xb)=|u_1(t^{n+1},\xb)|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$. The key is to calculate the oscillatory integral, \beq\int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \frac{1}{\left|\xb-b(s)\right|}ds\equiv \int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \frac{1}{\left|\xb-e(s)\sin(2\pi\og s)\right|}ds,\ee where $|\og|\gg1$, particularly due to the occurrence of the singularity in the kernel. Therefore, we use a regularization technique. For example, we could take \beq\int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \frac{1}{\left|\xb-b(s)\right|}ds\approx \int_{t}^{t+\btu t}\Phi^\eta \(\frac{1}{\left|\xb-b(s)\right|}\)ds,\ee where \[\Phi^\eta \(\frac{1}{\left|\xb-b(s)\right|}\)=\(\frac{2}{\eta}\)^{\frac{3}{2}} \int_{\R^3}e^{-2\pi\frac{|\xb-\xb'|^2}{\eta}}\frac{1}{\left|\xb'-b(s)\right|}d\xb'.\]
nodes.statement_short: Strang-type operator splitting: solve the free Schr\"odinger part by FFT pseudo-spectral propagation, then integrate the Hartree/Coulomb/nonlinear potential ODE exactly, with Gaussian regularization of the singular oscillatory Coulomb integral.
nodes.origin_citation: Bao, Jin & Markowich 2002; Huang, Jin, Markowich, Sparber & Zheng 2005
output: the value of $u_1$ at new time $t^{n+1}$

nodes.name: Step 1: free Schrodinger propagation by pseudo-spectral method
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \I \partial _t u_1 = -\, \btu u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{pseudo-spectral} method. Thus we can get the value of $u_1$ at new time $t^{n+1}$ by \[u^{n+1}_1=\(e^{-\I\btu t |\xi|^2}\hat{u}_1^{n}(\xi)\)^\vee,\] here `$\wedge$' and `$\vee$' denote the Fourier and inverse Fourier transform respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Advance the kinetic (Laplacian) part exactly in Fourier space.

nodes.name: Compute the Hartree potential from the density
nodes.statement: Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\xb)=|u_1(t^{n+1},\xb)|^2$, then we compute the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}(t^{n+1},\xb)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\]
nodes.statement_short: Solve the Poisson problem for $V_{Hartree}$ by dividing the density's Fourier transform by $|\xi|^2$.

nodes.name: Step 2: exact integration of the potential/nonlinear ODE
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2.} We solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\I \partial _tu_2  = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\xb)-a|u_2|^\sg\right)u_2, \quad u_2(t^{n},\xb)=u_1(t^{n+1},\xb), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\xb)$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}. It is easy to check that in this step the density $\rho(t,\xb)\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\xb)$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\btu t,\xb)=u_2(t,\xb)\,\exp\({\dpm-\I \int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \left(C_1V_{Hartree}(\xb)+V(s,\xb)-a\rho^\frac{\sg}{2}(\xb)\right) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\xb)=|u_1(t^{n+1},\xb)|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the potential step exactly as a pointwise phase multiplication, since the density is unchanged.

nodes.name: Regularization of the singular oscillatory Coulomb integral
nodes.statement: The key is to calculate the oscillatory integral, \beq\int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \frac{1}{\left|\xb-b(s)\right|}ds\equiv \int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \frac{1}{\left|\xb-e(s)\sin(2\pi\og s)\right|}ds,\ee where $|\og|\gg1$, particularly due to the occurrence of the singularity in the kernel. Therefore, we use a regularization technique. For example, we could take \beq\int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \frac{1}{\left|\xb-b(s)\right|}ds\approx \int_{t}^{t+\btu t}\Phi^\eta \(\frac{1}{\left|\xb-b(s)\right|}\)ds,\ee where \[\Phi^\eta \(\frac{1}{\left|\xb-b(s)\right|}\)=\(\frac{2}{\eta}\)^{\frac{3}{2}} \int_{\R^3}e^{-2\pi\frac{|\xb-\xb'|^2}{\eta}}\frac{1}{\left|\xb'-b(s)\right|}d\xb'.\]
nodes.statement_short: Mollify the singular Coulomb kernel by Gaussian convolution $\Phi^\eta$ before integrating in time.

nodes.name: Energy of the fast-potential model
nodes.statement: The energies for two models are \beq E^\og(t)\df\int_{\R^3}\(|\btd u^\omega|^2+\frac{C_1}{2}|\btd V_{Hartree}^\omega|^2 +cV^\og|u^\omega|^2-a\frac{2}{\sg+2}|u^\omega|^{\sg+2}\)d\xb, \ee
nodes.statement_short: Total energy $E^\og$ of the oscillatory model: kinetic + Hartree + Coulomb - local nonlinear contributions.

nodes.name: Energy of the time-averaged model
nodes.statement: \beq E(t)\df\int_{\R^3}\(|\btd u|^2+\frac{C_1}{2}|\btd V_{Hartree}|^2+{c}\langle V\rangle|u|^2-a\frac{2}{\sg+2}|u|^{\sg+2}\)d\xb, \ee respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Total energy $E$ of the time-averaged model, with $\langle V\rangle$ in place of $V^\og$.

nodes.name: Total mass
nodes.statement: \beq M(t)\df\int_{\R^3}|u(t,\xb)|^2d\xb, \ee

nodes.name: Conservation of the total mass in both models
nodes.statement: The total mass \beq M(t)\df\int_{\R^3}|u(t,\xb)|^2d\xb, \ee is conserved in both models.
nodes.statement_short: The $L^2$ mass is conserved for both the fast-potential and the time-averaged model.

nodes.name: Fast-potential model with an external potential
nodes.statement: If we consider an external potential $V_{ext}\(\xb\)$ in the equation \eqref{eq000} \cite{Fri,MT}, we have \[ i\eps\partial_t\psi=(i\eps\nabla-A)^2\psi+V_{ext}(\xb)\psi+c\frac{1}{|\xb|}\psi+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|\psi|^2)\psi -a|\psi|^\sigma\psi, \] by the same transformation \eqref{eqlenrd} and by fixing $\eps=1$, we obtain the following equation \begin{equation} i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V_{ext}\(\xb-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u +C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Oscillatory model augmented by a shifted external potential $V_{ext}(\xb-b(t))$.

nodes.name: Time-averaged model with an external potential
nodes.statement: and its time-averaged problem is \begin{equation} i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V_{ext}\rangle u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Averaged counterpart of the external-potential model, with $\langle V_{ext}\rangle$ and $\langle V\rangle$.

nodes.name: Time-averaged external potential
nodes.statement: with \[\langle V_{ext}\rangle(t,\xb) = \dpm\int\limits_{-\frac{1}2}^{{\frac{1}2}} V_{ext}\left(\xb-e(t) \sin(2\pi  s)\right) ds.\]

nodes.name: Periodic lattice potential
nodes.statement: In particular, if we consider a case with an periodic potential $V_\Gm\(\xb\)$ \cite{Fri,MT}, \ie $V_\Gm(\yb)$ is periodic w.r.t to a regular lattice $\Gm$, \[V_\Gm(\yb+\gm)=V_\Gm(\yb), \quad \fa \gm\in\Gm, \yb\in \R^3,\]
differentia: periodic w.r.t to a regular lattice $\Gm$

nodes.name: Fast-potential model with periodic lattice potential
nodes.statement: the above two equations \eqref{ext-fast}--\eqref{ext-avr} become \begin{equation} i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V_\Gm\(\xb-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u +C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Oscillatory model with the lattice potential $V_\Gm$ evaluated at the shifted position.

nodes.name: Time-averaged model with periodic lattice potential
nodes.statement: and its time-averaged problem is \begin{equation} i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V_\Gm\rangle\(t,\xb\) u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Averaged lattice model, with $\langle V_\Gm\rangle$ and $\langle V\rangle$.

nodes.name: Time-averaged lattice potential
nodes.statement: with \[\langle V_{\Gm}\rangle(t,\xb) = \dpm\int\limits_{-\frac{1}2}^{{\frac{1}2}} V_{\Gm}\left(\xb-e(t) \sin(2\pi  s)\right) ds.\]

nodes.name: Bloch-decomposition based time-splitting spectral algorithm
nodes.statement: We solve \eqref{bloch-fast} or \eqref{bloch-avr} by using the \emph{Bloch-decomposition based time-splitting method}, see \cite{HJMS, HJMS-2}. \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \I \partial _t u_1 = -\, \btu u_1 +V_\Gm\(t,\xb\) u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{Bloch-decomposition based pseudo-spectral} method. Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\xb)=|u_1(t^{n+1},\xb)|^2$, then we obtain the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}\(t^{n+1},\xb\)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\] \textbf{Step 2.} Then, we solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\I \partial _tu_2  = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\xb)-a|u_2|^\sg\right)u_2, \quad u_2\(t^{n},\xb\)=u_1\(t^{n+1},\xb\), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\xb)$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}. It is easy to check that  in this step the density $\rho(t,\xb)\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\xb)$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\btu t,\xb)=u_2(t,\xb)\,\exp\({\dpm-\I \int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \(C_1V_{Hartree}(\xb)+V(s,\xb)-a\rho^\frac{\sg}{2}(\xb)\) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\xb)=\left|u_1(t^{n+1},\xb)\right|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.statement_short: Same splitting as the pseudo-spectral scheme, but the kinetic-plus-lattice sub-problem is propagated in the Bloch eigenbasis of the periodic potential.

nodes.name: Step 1: kinetic plus lattice propagation in the Bloch basis
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \I \partial _t u_1 = -\, \btu u_1 +V_\Gm\(t,\xb\) u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{Bloch-decomposition based pseudo-spectral} method.
nodes.statement_short: Advance the linear part including the periodic potential $V_\Gm$ using the Bloch decomposition.

nodes.name: Compute the Hartree potential from the density
nodes.statement: Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\xb)=|u_1(t^{n+1},\xb)|^2$, then we obtain the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}\(t^{n+1},\xb\)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\]
nodes.statement_short: Recover $V_{Hartree}$ from the updated density through the Fourier-space Poisson solve.

nodes.name: Step 2: exact integration of the potential/nonlinear ODE
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2.} Then, we solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\I \partial _tu_2  = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\xb)-a|u_2|^\sg\right)u_2, \quad u_2\(t^{n},\xb\)=u_1\(t^{n+1},\xb\), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\xb)$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}. It is easy to check that  in this step the density $\rho(t,\xb)\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\xb)$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\btu t,\xb)=u_2(t,\xb)\,\exp\({\dpm-\I \int_{t}^{t+\btu t} \(C_1V_{Hartree}(\xb)+V(s,\xb)-a\rho^\frac{\sg}{2}(\xb)\) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\xb)=\left|u_1(t^{n+1},\xb)\right|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the Hartree/Coulomb/nonlinear potential step exactly as a phase multiplication.

nodes.name: Comparison of the two algorithms
nodes.statement: Certainly, if there is no lattice potential $V_\Gamma$, the above two algorithms are coincided with each other. But we must include the lattice potential $V_\Gamma$ when the interaction with laser or other lattice potenital are not eligible. We will see that the Bloch-decomposition based method is much more efficient in the case with lattice potential $V_\Gamma$ than the traditional pseudo-spectral method (\cf Fig. \ref{Fig012}-\ref{Fig013}), \ie we could use much larger mesh size than the traditional pseudo-spectral method to get the same accuracy.
nodes.statement_short: The two schemes agree without a lattice potential; with one, the Bloch-based scheme allows much coarser meshes for the same accuracy.

nodes.name: Example 3.1: convergence to the time-averaged model
nodes.statement: Here we set the semiclassical parameter $\eps=1$, $e(t)=(0,0,1)^T$, $\sigma=\frac{2}{3}$, $a=50$, $C_1=20$, $c=1$. We compare the time-averaged model with the fast-potential model for different values of $\og$. We choose appropriate constants $C_1$ and $c$ to make the two potential components in the energy comparable.
nodes.statement_short: Benchmark comparison of the two models for $\og=5,10,20,40$ in the mass-subcritical case $\sigma=2/3$.

nodes.name: Observed convergence of energy and wave function
nodes.statement: From Figures \ref{Fig001}--\ref{Fig002}, we can see that as $|\og|\to\infty$, the average of the energy $E^\og(t)$ converges to the energy $E(t)$ of time-averaged model. The corresponding wave-function $u^\og(t,\xb)$ also converges to $u(t,\xb)$ at least in $L^2$-norm. Figure \ref{Fig002} also shows the conservation of $E(t)$ and $M(t)$.

nodes.name: Example 3.2: blow-up tests
nodes.statement: Here we consider an example with $\eps=1$, $e(t)=(0,0,1)^T$, $a=50$, $C_1=100$, $c=0.1$. We start the time-averaged model from a ground state for $\sg=2/3$ (\cf plot (a) in Fig. \ref{Fig003}). Then we consider \eqref{eq:fast} with a mass supercritical power-type nonlinearity, i.e. $\sg>4/3$, we analyse the blow-up of the norm \beq\|\btd u\|_{L^2}=\left(\int_{\R^3}|\btd u(t,\xb)|^2d\xb\right)^{1/2}.\ee
nodes.statement_short: Mass-supercritical runs ($\sg>4/3$) started from a ground state, tracking blow-up of $\|\btd u\|_{L^2}$.

nodes.name: H^1 seminorm used to monitor blow-up
nodes.statement: \beq\|\btd u\|_{L^2}=\left(\int_{\R^3}|\btd u(t,\xb)|^2d\xb\right)^{1/2}.\ee

nodes.name: Blow-up time decreases with the nonlinearity exponent
nodes.statement: In Fig. \ref{Fig003}--\ref{Fig004}, we can see that the blow-up time decreases as $\sg$ increases.

nodes.name: Agreement of the two models near blow-up: supercritical vs subcritical
nodes.statement: Comparing the $L^2$ norms of the gradient of the wave-function for the time averaged model and the fast model in the blow up test we can see that they are very similar in the super-critical case (\cf Figures \ref{Fig005}--\ref{Fig006} and Figures \ref{Fig003}--\ref{Fig004}). They exhibit more differences in the subcritical case (see Fig. \ref{Fig007}--\ref{Fig008}).
nodes.statement_short: $\|\btd u\|_{L^2}$ of the two models nearly coincides in the supercritical case but differs more in the subcritical case.

nodes.name: Early-stage impact of the Coulomb potential on the wave packet
nodes.statement: Furthermore, from Figures \ref{Fig009}--\ref{Fig009-1}, we can see that the Coulomb potential significantly impacts the wave packet at the early stage. This becomes particularly clear with slower blow-up and smaller frequency $\og$.

nodes.name: Example 3.3: particle shot towards the field with a harmonic trap
nodes.statement: Here we are interested in the patterns of interaction of the magnetic field with the particle, especially when a particle is shot towards the field, and scattered by it. We set $e=(0,0,1)^T$ in eq. (\ref{eq:fast-p}), and choose an initial datum of the form \[ u_0(\xb)=e^{-4|\xb-(1,1,0)^T|^2+ i (x_1-x_2)}, \quad \mbox{ for } \xb=(x_1,x_2,x_3)^T. \] In this example, we add a harmonic trap potential \[V(\xb)=50|\xb|^2,\] \ie the equation in \eqref{eq:fast} becomes \begin{equation} i\d_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V\(\xb-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u^\omega +C_1(|\cdot|\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Scattering experiment: a moving Gaussian wave packet in a harmonic trap interacting with the oscillating field.
nodes.section: 3.1.3 Interaction of the magnetic field with the particle

nodes.name: Wave packet motion under the trap
nodes.statement: The results are shown in Figure \ref{Fig010}. We can see that the wave packet moves under the interaction with the trap $V(\xb)$.
nodes.section: 3.1.3 Interaction of the magnetic field with the particle

nodes.name: Example 3.4: time-dependent vector e(t)
nodes.statement: We consider a time-dependent vector $e(t)=(-1,-1,-1)\sin 2\pi t$ in eq. (\ref{eq:fast-p}), and an initial datum of the form \[ u_0(x)=e^{-4|\xb|^2}. \]

nodes.name: Mild effect of a slowly varying e(t)
nodes.statement: The results are shown in Figure \ref{Fig011}. As $e(t)$ is slowly varying in time, its effects are not very pronounced except when $e(t)$ is close to 0.

nodes.name: Example 3.5: interaction with a periodic lattice
nodes.statement: Finally, we consider a case with periodic lattice, \ie the equation in \eqref{eq:fast} becomes \begin{equation} i\d_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V^\omega u^\omega+V_\Gm\(\xb-b(t)\)u^\omega +C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega, \end{equation} and its time-averaged problem is \begin{equation} i\d_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V\rangle u+\langle V_\Gamma\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u. \end{equation} We also take the initial datum of the form \[ u_0(x)=e^{-4|\xb|^2}. \] Here $V_\Gm(\yb)$ is periodic w.r.t to a regular lattice $\Gm$, \[V_\Gm(\yb+\gm)=V_\Gm(\yb), \quad \fa \gm\in\Gm,\ \yb\in \R^3.\] For sake of simplicity, we choose \[V_\Gm(\yb)=\sum_{l=1}^3 \sin^2(\og_l y_l), \quad \mbox{ for }\yb=(y_1,y_2,y_3)^T\in\R^3, \] with $\og_1=\og_2=\og_3=2\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: Lattice experiment with $V_\Gm(\yb)=\sum_{l=1}^3\sin^2(2\pi y_l)$ and a centred Gaussian initial datum.

nodes.name: Lattice interaction and efficiency of the Bloch-based scheme
nodes.statement: The results are shown in Figures \ref{Fig012}-\ref{Fig013}. We can see the interaction between the lattice potential and the wave packet. Certainly, the wave function of the fast model is more peaked than the solution of the time-averaged model. From these figures, we can also find that the Bloch-decomposition based algorithm is more efficient than traditional pseudo-spectral method in this case.
nodes.statement_short: With a lattice, the fast model stays more peaked than the averaged one and the Bloch-based scheme outperforms the plain pseudo-spectral one.

nodes.name: Stability of the XFEL equation under perturbations of the potential
nodes.statement:
Let $V, 	ilde V$ be two potentials such that $V, 	ilde V\in L^\infty(\R; L^{ rac{3}{1+3\delta}}(\R^3)+L^{ rac{3}{1-3\delta}}(\R^3))$, $
abla V, 
abla	ilde V\in L^\infty(\R; L^{ rac{3}{2+3\delta}}(\R^3)+L^{ rac{3}{2-3\delta}}(\R^3))$, for some $\delta>0$ small. Let $u, 	ilde u$ be the solutions of the Cauchy problems  egin{equation*} \left\{ egin{aligned} &i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+V u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u\ &u(t,\xb) ig|_{t=0}=u_0(\xb), \end{aligned}ight. \end{equation*}   with the potential $V$ and respectively with $V$ replaced by $	ilde V$, and initial data $u_0$ and, respectively $	ilde u_0\in H^1(\R^3)$, respectively. Let $0<T<\min\{T_{max}, 	ilde T_{max}\}$, where $T_{max}, 	ilde T_{max}$ are the maximal existence times for $u, 	ilde u$, respectively. Then, for any admissible pair $(q, r)$, we have  egin{equation} \|u-	ilde u\|_{L^q((0, T); W^{1, r}(\R^3))}\leq C\pare{ \|u_0-	ilde u_0\|_{H^1}+\|V-	ilde V\|_{L^\infty_t(L^{ rac{3}{1+3\delta}}_x+L^{ rac{3}{1-3\delta}}_x)} +\|
abla(V-	ilde V)\|_{L^\infty_t(L^{ rac{3}{2+3\delta}}_x+L^{ rac{3}{2-3\delta}}_x)}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Solutions depend Lipschitz-continuously, in Strichartz norms, on the initial datum and on the potential (with its gradient) in the stated Lebesgue-sum spaces.
assumptions: Let $V, \tilde V$ be two potentials such that $V, \tilde V\in L^\infty(\R; L^{\frac{3}{1+3\delta}}(\R^3)+L^{\frac{3}{1-3\delta}}(\R^3))$
$\nabla V, \nabla\tilde V\in L^\infty(\R; L^{\frac{3}{2+3\delta}}(\R^3)+L^{\frac{3}{2-3\delta}}(\R^3))$, for some $\delta>0$ small

Let $u, \tilde u$ be the solutions of the Cauchy problems \begin{equation*} \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+V u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u\\ &u(t,\xb)\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\xb), \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation*} with the potential $V$ and respectively with $V$ replaced by $\tilde V$, and initial data $u_0$ and, respectively $\tilde u_0\in H^1(\R^3)$, respectively
Let $0<T<\min\{T_{max}, \tilde T_{max}\}$, where $T_{max}, \tilde T_{max}$ are the maximal existence times for $u, \tilde u$, respectively
conclusions: $\|u-\tilde u\|_{L^q((0, T); W^{1, r}(\R^3))}\leq C\pare{ \|u_0-\tilde u_0\|_{H^1}+\|V-\tilde V\|_{L^\infty_t(L^{\frac{3}{1+3\delta}}_x+L^{\frac{3}{1-3\delta}}_x)} +\|\nabla(V-\tilde V)\|_{L^\infty_t(L^{\frac{3}{2+3\delta}}_x+L^{\frac{3}{2-3\delta}}_x)}}$

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the stability estimate
nodes.statement: The proof is indeed quite standard, as similar results are well known in the literature, see below for the references. The proof of stability of equation \eqref{eq:fast} with respect to perturbations of the potential is done by adapting in a straightforward way the local well-posedness result. For furhter details we refer the reader to \cite{Kato87}, \cite{Caz} Section 4.
nodes.statement_short: Adapt the standard local well-posedness (Strichartz/fixed-point) argument for nonlinear Schrodinger equations to potential perturbations, following Kato and Cazenave.
